name: parasail
baseline: SSW (Complete-Striped-Smith-Waterman-Library, C, SSE2 striped Smith-Waterman); the same page also times Opal, SWIPE and ssearch36
workload: Score-only Smith-Waterman search of four query sequences (110, 195, 390 and 513 residues) against UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot (547,964 sequences), BLOSUM50, gap open 3, gap extend 1, one thread, mean of three runs, whole-database wall time in seconds.
claimed_speedup: performance.md, Intel Haswell E5-2670 v3 table (seconds per database search for the 110/195/390/513-residue queries): SSW (SSE2) 12.0 / 25.6 / 41.5 / 48.7; parasail AVX2 16-bit 9.3 / 12.0 / 17.4 / 21.5 (about 1.3x, 2.1x, 2.4x and 2.3x faster than SSW, derived from page data); parasail SSE4.1 16-bit 10.8 / 15.9 / 27.4 / 33.8 (about 1.1x to 1.6x, derived from page data). MacBook Pro i5 table: SSW (SSE2) 13.2 / 27.1 / 41.7 / 52.4 vs parasail SSE4.1 16-bit 11.3 / 15.9 / 25.8 / 36.9. SWIPE (SSSE3) is faster than parasail SSE4.1 on both machines (9.6 / 16.5 / 30.9 / 39.9 s on Haswell).
compiler_and_flags: Haswell table: Intel ICC 15.0.1, -O3. MacBook table: Apple LLVM 6.0 (clang-600.0.57), flags not stated. Command lines are given: parasail_aligner -x -t 1 -a sw_striped_profile_avx2_256_16 -o 3 -e 1 -m blosum50 -f uniprot_sprot -q <query>; ssw_test -p uniprot_sprot.fasta <query>.
hardware: Haswell table: Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 at 2.3 GHz, 64 GB DDR4-2133. Second table: MacBook Pro, Intel i5 at 2.53 GHz, 8 GB (SSE4.1 only).
tradeoffs: C99 library with SSE2, SSE4.1, AVX2, AltiVec and NEON kernels (README), many striped, scan and diagonal variants for global, semi-global and local alignment, with optional statistics or SAM CIGAR traceback (slower than score-only). Several 8-bit, 16-bit and saturating-width variants must be chosen by the user; the 8-bit 'sat' variants fall back to 16-bit on overflow. Language bindings are listed in the README (Python via parasail-python, Rust, Java).
caveats: The win is against SSW only in the narrow sense of a 2015-era SSE2 kernel: AVX2 rows compare different instruction sets than SSW's SSE2, and the build flags of SSW, Opal and SWIPE are not stated. SWIPE (a database-search specialist) stays faster than parasail SSE4.1, and parasail's 8-bit 'sat' SSE4.1 variant is slower than SSW at the longer queries on Haswell (55.2 s vs 48.7 s at 513 residues). Only scores are computed, not alignments or tracebacks. The Swiss-Prot release is not stated. No SeqAn or scalar Smith-Waterman row appears on the page. The BMC Bioinformatics 2016 paper was not opened (NCBI blocked); a search-result summary only says SWIPE is 1.2 to 2.4 times faster than parasail for sequences under 500 residues and parasail is faster for longer ones (snippet, not verified). The license is a custom Battelle BSD-style text (permits use, copy, modify and sell) that is not an SPDX-listed or OSI-listed license and requires citing the 2016 paper in publications. Last commit seen on the master branch; the develop branch was not checked.

name: ksw2
baseline: parasail (global Needleman-Wunsch, striped/scan/diagonal SIMD variants) and ksw2's own scalar Green-formulation DP (ksw2_gg)
workload: Global affine-gap alignment of two long DNA sequence pairs (a 50k pair and a 16.5k pair in the repo's test directory), wall time in seconds, score-only or with CIGAR as marked in the table.
claimed_speedup: README Performance Analysis table, 50k pair, global score-only: ksw2 scalar `-t gg -s` 7.3 s; parasail `ps_nw_striped_32` (SSE4) 2.2 s, SSE2 striped 2.9 s, scan and diag 3.0 s; ksw2 `-t extz2_sse -sg` 0.96 s (SSE2) and 0.84 s (SSE4) (about 2.6x faster than parasail's best row and 8.7x faster than scalar gg for SSE4, derived from page data). With extension and Z-drop (`-t extz2_sse -s`) 3.0 s (SSE2) and 2.7 s (SSE4), which is slower than parasail's 2.2 s global row. 16.5k pair with CIGAR: `-t gg` 1.6 s, `-t extz2_sse` 0.40 s (about 4x, derived), `-t extz2_sse -g` 0.18 s.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile default: gcc -g -Wall -Wextra -Wc++-compat -O2 -march=native (SSE4.1 when available; `make sse2=1` for SSE2 only). The README does not say which compiler or flags produced the table.
tradeoffs: Global alignment and extension (Z-drop) only, no local alignment; SSE2 and SSE4.1 intrinsics documented in the README (the Makefile only offers an avx2=1 compile flag, no NEON); fixed banding; affine and dual (two-piece) affine gap costs; supports CIGAR with left or right gap alignment. Suzuki-Kasahara diagonal formulation needs a single match score and a single mismatch score.
caveats: No CPU model is stated for the timing table, so tier C. The README itself says KSW2 is faster than parasail 'partly because' KSW2 uses one score for all matches and another for mismatches while parasail takes a generic matrix, so the comparison is not the same task. Rows differ in what they compute (score-only global vs extension with Z-drop; the parasail rows do not list `-s`), and only the global score-only row beats parasail. Test data are checked in (test/ has MT-human.fa, MT-orang.fa, q1.fa, t1.fa and gzipped q2 and t2; which files are the 50k and 16.5k pairs was not confirmed) so the table can be rerun on your own CPU. Last commit 2023-06-27 (about 3.3 years ago); minimap2 carries its own copy of these sources. The Suzuki-Kasahara BMC Bioinformatics 2018 and minimap2 Bioinformatics 2018 papers were not opened.

name: WFA2-lib
baseline: KSW2 (ksw2_extz2_sse, exact unbanded gap-affine DP with CIGAR); the artifact also times edlib, BitPAl and WFA-LM
workload: Exact gap-affine alignment (penalties 0,4,6,2, CIGAR output) of long real sequence pairs: 1,326 ONT-region pairs and 1,991 ONT MinION ultra-long read pairs (hsapiens HG002/CHM13 data), per-pair time in ms from the BiWFA paper artifact's statistics_all.tsv.gz.
claimed_speedup: No comparison numbers in the WFA2-lib README or tools README (the tools README only shows a sample align_benchmark run of 5M 100 bp pairs on an unnamed machine). From the BiWFA paper artifact data (smarco/BiWFA-paper evaluation/data, matched pairs, ratios computed by me from the raw per-pair time_ms rows, derived from page data): total time of ksw2-extz2-sse divided by WFA2 default high-memory mode is 7.26x on the 1,326 ONT-region pairs (median per-pair ratio 12.2x, WFA2 faster on 99% of pairs) and 7.51x on the 1,991 MinION ultra-long pairs (median per-pair ratio 4.6x, WFA2 faster on about 100% of pairs at two-decimal rounding); BiWFA (O(s) memory) is 9.95x and 9.76x faster in total time than ksw2; the medium-memory mode is 2.6x and 2.0x faster than ksw2. The alignment scores agree with ksw2 on all 3,317 pairs compared. WFA2 high-memory mode is also 3.0x faster than WFA-LM, but edlib (edit distance only, not gap-affine) is faster than every WFA2 mode (about 9x faster than the high-memory mode in total time on the first set, derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.0 (module load gcc/10.2.0 in evaluation/0_Preparation.md); BiWFA-paper Makefile 'all' target adds -O3 -march=native to CC_FLAGS=-Wall -g; benchmark branch pinned at commit d5532da; ksw2 run through the artifact's align_benchmark with ksw2_bandwidth -1 and zdrop -1 (no banding).
hardware: Cluster jobs submitted with sbatch -c 128 --exclusive (a 128-hardware-thread node per job, one alignment at a time in the script loop); CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Exact algorithm whose time is O(ns+s^2) in score s: huge wins on similar sequences, shrinking as divergence grows. Default high-memory mode needs O(s^2) memory; low, ultralow (BiWFA, O(s) memory) and heuristic modes trade time for memory or accuracy. Gap-linear, gap-affine and dual-gap affine costs with end-to-end and ends-free (semi-global, glocal, extension) modes per the README; local Smith-Waterman is not listed. Plain C with compiler auto-vectorisation rather than intrinsics, so no ISA-specific code. C++ and Rust bindings.
caveats: The measured code is the BiWFA-paper snapshot (benchmark branch commit d5532da), not the current WFA2-lib main, and the data are long noisy reads at small divergence where WFA's O(ns) behaviour is most favourable; short reads or highly divergent pairs will show other ratios. CPU model is missing, so tier B (peer-reviewed artifact of the Bioinformatics 2023 BiWFA paper) not A. I did not open the papers (NCBI and DOI blocked); a search snippet of the WFA Bioinformatics 2021 abstract reports 20-300x faster on short Illumina-like reads and 10-100x on ONT reads (snippet only, not verified here). The time_ms column comes from the repo's log2info.py extraction, which I did not open, so what the timer includes (alignment only or whole process) and what `--repeat 100000` does are unverified; the same column feeds both tools so ratios hold, but absolute times may include setup. The memory_kb column looked inconsistent and was not used. The tools/ README in the repo says the full external comparison lives on the `benchmark` branch. Edlib solves edit distance only and is faster than all WFA2 modes in this data.

name: libstats
baseline: scalar loops over std::exp, std::log, std::erf and std::cos (platform libm); corvus v1.0.1 SIMD kernels on M1 as a second baseline
workload: tools/simd_verification primitive benchmark: 1,024-element double arrays (linspace inputs, exp over [-500, 500]), scalar std:: loop vs libstats VectorOps::vector_exp/log/erf/cos, 5 timed iterations after a warm-up; corvus issue #43 compares ns per element at n = 1e6 through libstats VectorOps.
claimed_speedup: docs/SIMD_BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md 'Representative v1.5.x' primitive speedups over the scalar libm loop: AVX2+FMA VectorExp 3.4x, VectorLog 1.7x, VectorErf 2.5x, VectorCos 4.9x; NEON 2.1x, 1.8x, 8.0x, 3.0x; AVX-512 5.0x, 3.9x, 1.3x, 8.5x. Current v2.x NEON exp: 2.5-2.6x (was 2.1x) on a Mac Mini M1 after the table-gather kernel. corvus issue #43 (owner's own M1 table, ns per element at n = 1e6): libstats exp 1.0 vs corvus 4.6, log 1.7 vs 13.7, cos/sin 2.5 vs 4.1, erf 1.4 vs 2.3 (corvus later improved to exp 2.4, log 3.9, erf 1.8, cos/sin 2.6 ns).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the primitive table; the doc says to use Release builds (cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release). The accuracy section mentions MSVC on the Windows Zen 4 machine and AppleClang on the Mac.
hardware: Intel Core i7-7820HQ (Kaby Lake, AVX2+FMA), Mac Mini Apple M1 (NEON) and AMD Ryzen 7 7445HS (Zen 4, AVX-512) are the validation machines; the v1.5.x primitive table does not say which machine produced which row.
tradeoffs: The SIMD kernels are internal to a statistical-distributions library (SSE2, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON; SLEEF-inspired exp/log, musl-style erf, a 7-term Horner cos), not a standalone libm replacement. Needs array-style batch calls. Kernel accuracy is looser than a correctly rounded libm.
caveats: Own-benchmark numbers on a tiny, cache-resident array (1,024 doubles, 5 iterations) with no compiler version or flags, so tier C. The v1.5.x table is labelled by the doc as historical. The accuracy gap weakens the comparison: simd_verification accepts cos to 1e-9 (7-term polynomial, max error about 1e-10) and the corvus owner declined to adopt libstats' roughly 0.52 ULP kernels because corvus keeps correctly rounded bounds, so a 4.9x cos result is not like for like with libm. The libm baseline is whatever the build platform ships (MSVC UCRT, Apple libm, glibc), and glibc was not named. The corvus comparison is from an issue by the same author and compares libstats against corvus at its earlier state; corvus's own PERFORMANCE document is the better reference for corvus vs libm. 1-star repository maintained by one author.

name: bolt
baseline: Eigen dense float matrix multiply (`out.noalias() = X * Q`, the repo's 'matmul' rows; README and slides call it BLAS) and the repo's own product quantization (PQ, OPQ) encoders; FAISS is not benchmarked
workload: experiments/results (C++ Catch profile tests, 10 repetitions x 5 trials): square float32 matrix multiply of N x N matrices for N = 64 ... 8192 with Bolt approximate multiplication (8, 16 or 32 byte codes, with and without encoding the matrix), plus encoding and distance-scan timings for 10,000-vector batches of 128-dimensional vectors and 16-byte codes.
claimed_speedup: README: Bolt 'can probably save you 10-200x space and compute time'; slides (assets/bolt-slides.pdf): 10x faster than PQ/OPQ and 100x faster than raw floats for distance computation, matrix multiply faster than BLAS even when encoding first. Result files, medians of the listed trials (derived from page data): Eigen matmul 0.054 ms (N=128), 0.405 ms (256), 3.1 ms (512), 25.1 ms (1024), 203 ms (2048), 1,654 ms (4096), 13,190 ms (8192); Bolt<8> without matrix encoding 0.040, 0.137, 0.54, 2.2, 11.2, 46.8, 231 ms (1.4x, 3.0x, 5.8x, 11x, 18x, 35x, 57x faster) and Bolt<8> with encoding 0.067, 0.226, 0.92, 3.7, 17.4, 77.5, 350 ms (0.8x, 1.8x, 3.4x, 6.7x, 12x, 21x, 38x). Below N = 128 Bolt is slower than Eigen (N = 64: 0.024 ms vs 0.009 ms with encoding). Encoding 10,000 128-dimensional vectors into 16 bytes (D=128, M=16 file): PQ 39.8 ms, OPQ 46.2 ms vs Bolt 2.29 ms (about 17x vs PQ); query lookup-table build 34.7 ms (PQ float) vs 1.42 ms (Bolt, about 24x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the result files. experiments/README says Bolt has only been tested with Clang on OS X and that the paper's timings come from Xcode builds, not the Bazel build in the repo; flags not given. AVX2 required.
tradeoffs: Lossy: Bolt approximates distances and dot products with learned 4-bit codebooks (error bounded in the paper's theory), needs a training pass (k-means) before encoding, and is only worthwhile for large collections of mostly dense vectors. AVX2 only, no ARM port. Python wrapper is reported as no longer building for many users and is slower than the C++ path. The MADDNESS successor ('mithral') is in the same repo.
caveats: First-party raw timing outputs with no CPU model and no compiler flags, so tier C even though a peer-reviewed KDD 2017 paper exists (arXiv and the ACM copy were not reachable; the paper's claimed hardware and baselines were not verified, and a search snippet confirms only the abstract claims of 12x faster compression and up to 10x faster distance and dot-product operations). The Python README example says '~10x here' for numpy dot products, not C++ numbers. The Bolt matmul rows use random codes, random centroids and random lookup tables (cpp/test/quantize/profile_bolt.cpp) and measure speed only; approximation quality is evaluated separately in Python. The 'BLAS' baseline is Eigen's own GEMM (single or multi-threaded not stated in the files opened), so it is not an MKL or OpenBLAS comparison. The checked-in timing files contain no PQ scan row, so the 10x-vs-PQ scan claim in the slides could not be reproduced from the files; only the encoding and lookup-table rows could. Last commit 2022-06-24.

name: Quicker ADC (faiss-quickeradc)
baseline: FAISS PQ ADC (IndexPQ-style m x 8 float lookup-table scan, FAISS as of mid-2018) and polysemous codes
workload: Exhaustive nearest-neighbour search on SIFT1M with 64-bit and 128-bit product-quantization codes: per-query time (ms) with R@1 and R@100; non-exhaustive IVF, Inverted Multi-Index and HNSW-IVF search on SIFT1000M and Deep1B as recall-vs-query-time curves.
claimed_speedup: Numbers read from the README table image img/exhaustive_search_sift1M.png (query time per query in ms): 64-bit codes: FAISS PQ m x 8 5.50 ms (R@1 0.227, R@100 0.918); polysemous 1.19 ms (0.225 / 0.854); Quicker ADC m x {8,8} AVX512 BW 1.18 ms (0.223 / 0.918), i.e. about 4.7x faster than FAISS PQ at equal R@100 (derived from page data); m x {6,6,4} AVX512 BW 0.56 ms (0.179 / 0.859, about 9.8x faster at lower recall); m x {4,4} AVX512 BW 0.58 ms (0.158 / 0.807, about 9.5x). 128-bit codes: FAISS PQ 9.51 ms (0.446 / 0.998); polysemous 2.90 ms; Quicker ADC m x {8,8} AVX512 BW 2.36 ms (0.446 / 0.997, about 4.0x); m x {6,6,4} 0.99 ms (0.371 / 0.984, about 9.6x); m x {4,4} AVX512 BW 0.80 ms (0.313 / 0.964, about 11.9x). The non-exhaustive SIFT1000M and Deep1B figures are curves with no printed numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; ./configure detects the CPU and enables SSE, AVX2 or AVX512 accordingly. Benchmarks run through benchs/bench_vpq_sift1000m.py and benchs/bench_vpq_1bn.py at code commit d11c5af.
hardware: README says 'AWS m5 instances' for the SIFT1000M and Deep1B plots; no CPU model for the SIFT1M exhaustive table (AVX512 BW needs a Skylake-SP class or newer CPU).
tradeoffs: L2 distance only; AVX512 BW needed for the fastest m x {8,8} and 6-bit variants, AVX2 and SSE variants exist; m x {8} VBMI timings could not be measured because no processor supported it at the time. Faster variants pay in recall (m x {4,4} loses about 0.07 R@1 and 0.11 R@100 vs PQ at 64 bits). Heavy template instantiation increases compile time. No OnDiskInvertedList support.
caveats: First-party table shown as an image, no CPU model or compiler, so tier C. The paper (arXiv 1812.09162, later IEEE TPAMI 2021 per the lead) was not opened because arXiv is blocked here; a search snippet confirms only that it reports outperforming FAISS and polysemous codes. The FAISS baseline is the mid-2018 FAISS this fork branched from (last upstream sync 2018-08-30), and later FAISS releases added their own 4-bit fast-scan PQ path (not checked this session), so the baseline is dated. At equal recall (m x {8,8}) the gain is about 4x to 5x; the 10x figures are at lower recall. The same table lists 'Sequential' float rows (for example 25.8 ms for m x {4,4}) that show the SIMD part, not a competitor. Licence is mixed: Thomson Licensing's changes are Clear BSD (explicitly no patent licence) on top of Facebook's BSD plus a PATENTS file inherited from FAISS (its terms were not read).

language: C (orlp/ed25519 compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten, JavaScript wrapper)

claimed_speedup: berith README Node table (Apple M1 Max): supercop.wasm 5.0.1 187.96 us/iter; @noble/curves 0.7.0 1.99 ms/iter (about 10.6x slower than supercop.wasm, derived from page data); node:crypto native 152.67 us/iter with unserialized keys (supercop.wasm about 1.23x slower, derived) and 555.61 us/iter serialized (supercop.wasm about 3.0x faster, derived); berith (Wasm) 281.68 us/iter, which the README itself reports as '0.67x faster than supercop.wasm'. The supercop.wasm README makes no speed claim (only 'multiple times smaller' than supercop.js).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the measured wasm (the npm 5.0.1 package is a prebuilt Emscripten build 'optimized for small size'); the benchmark itself is JavaScript run with node v18.12.1.
stars_or_usage: 13 stars; npm supercop.wasm 5.0.1 (2018-02-24) is the latest version
tradeoffs: The README states no constant-time or side-channel guarantees; it wraps orlp/ed25519, a small portable C implementation, and the measured wasm is slower than native node:crypto when keys are not serialized. Wasm module is small, works in browsers and Node with the supercop.js API (Uint8Array instead of Buffer).
caveats: Third-party benchmark in a competing library's repository (public code, CPU and Node version stated, but one machine, 1,000 samples and a mixed keygen+sign+verify iteration rather than separate operations), so tier B on the independent-benchmark route rather than A: the wasm build flags are not stated and berith is not a well-known suite. Neither tweetnacl-js nor the native SUPERCOP ed25519 build named in the lead appears in the table; the JS baseline is @noble/curves 0.7.0, and the native node:crypto row beats supercop.wasm when keys are not serialized. Last commit and last npm release both 2018-02-24, so the measured code is old and the repository is unmaintained.
